clinical_knowledge.topic: Congestive Heart Failure evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Congestive Heart Failure is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes obtaining BNP, chest X-ray, and echocardiography, and, because this is a young patient without typical risk factors, actively searching for a non-ischaemic cause (myocarditis, familial/genetic cardiomyopathy, thyroid disease, or substance use) rather than assuming ischaemic heart failure, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: progressive shortness of breath, ankle swelling, and fatigue for 1 month

Key HPI features: A 29-year-old male presents to the clinic with progressive shortness of breath, ankle swelling, and fatigue for 1 month, gradually worsening. He has no known prior heart disease, and denies any preceding viral illness, recreational drug use, or family history of heart problems that he is aware of.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals and volume status (JVP, lung crackles, peripheral oedema). Cardiac auscultation for S3 gallop or murmurs. BNP/NT-proBNP, chest X-ray, and echocardiogram to confirm heart failure and assess ejection fraction; in a young adult, also screen for treatable causes with TSH, viral serology history, and a family/substance-use history.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Congestive Heart Failure.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Breathlessness at rest, or waking at night gasping.
management_principles: Obtain BNP, chest X-ray, and echocardiogram; in a young adult without typical risk factors, screen for non-ischaemic causes (myocarditis, familial cardiomyopathy, thyroid disease, substance use)
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with chief complaint of progressive shortness of breath, ankle swelling, and fatigue for 1 month. HPI: systolic/diastolic dysfunction.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals and volume status (JVP, lung crackles, peripheral oedema). Cardiac auscultation for S3 gallop or murmurs. BNP/NT-proBNP, chest X-ray, and echocardiogram to confirm heart failure and assess ejection fraction; in a young adult, also screen for treatable causes with TSH, viral serology history, and a family/substance-use history.
reference_soap.assessment: New-onset Congestive Heart Failure in a 29-year-old man; given his age and absence of traditional cardiovascular risk factors, a non-ischaemic cause (myocarditis, familial/genetic dilated cardiomyopathy, thyroid disease, or substance-induced cardiomyopathy) must be actively sought rather than assumed to be ischaemic.
reference_soap.plan: Obtain BNP, chest X-ray, and echocardiogram; screen for non-ischaemic causes (myocarditis, familial cardiomyopathy, thyroid disease, substance use). Start oral Furosemide, titrate GDMT. Consult specialist if symptoms worsen. Counsel patient.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Congestive Heart Failure
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Congestive Heart Failure
Implement evidence-based management plan: Obtain BNP, chest X-ray, Echo. Start oral Furosemide, titrate GDMT

teaching.one_liner: The heart cannot pump enough for the body's needs, so fluid backs up — breathlessness, ankle swelling and fatigue together.
red_flags: Breathlessness at rest, or waking at night gasping

must_ask.say: How far can you walk on the flat before you need to stop?
Do you get breathless lying flat? How many pillows do you use?
Have your ankles or legs been swelling?
Do you wake in the night short of breath and have to sit up?
Has your weight gone up quickly in the last week or two?
What medications are you taking at the moment?

must_ask.objective: Possible cause in a young patient
must_ask.say: Have you had a recent viral illness, do you use any recreational drugs, or does anyone in your family have heart problems or an unexplained sudden death?
